extracted.intended_audience: patent prosecutors, in-house counsel, SEP portfolio managers, and IP/licensing professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on prosecuting, managing, licensing, and litigating standard-essential patents (SEPs) across jurisdictions and standards-setting organizations. Focuses on claim drafting, portfolio hygiene, declaration practices, FRAND licensing, royalty optimization, marking, and litigation/settlement considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align prosecution with SSO participation and timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful SEP prosecution often points toward participatory contributions in SSO meetings and patent application filings aligned with the SSO’s development stages to maximize claim mapping to mandatory standard features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different SSOs have differing procedures and timelines (e.g., ETSI/3GPP structured release cycles, IEEE rapid Wi‑Fi amendments, video coding standards with distinct codec tools). Consider filing patent applications before submitting contributions and reference evolving SSO documents precisely. Tailor prosecution strategy to the specific standard and SSO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting to cover multiple standard features (mandatory and key optional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applicants should draft claims to cover multiple technical features specified in the standards, targeting both mandatory and key optional features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To ensure claims read on applicable standards (to the extent predictable), internally maintain detailed and continuously updated claim charts during prosecution showing explicit references to relevant portions of the standards documents. Draft claims to target technically distinct tools in standards like video codecs and to encompass foreseeable standard permutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patenting emerging standards features (cover permutations and keep continuations)
rubrics_metrics.description: When filing patent applications covering proposals, applicants should attempt to cover all possible permutations and combinations of the proposed solutions and consider multiple parallel applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File multiple parallel applications covering different aspects of proposed solutions. Keep continuation, divisional, and reissue applications pending in multiple jurisdictions to capture emerging standards and variations thereof, given delays from proposal submission to adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synchronize prosecution across jurisdictions for overlapping claim scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Because technical standards are global while patent rights are national, developing SEP portfolios with strong overlapping claims across jurisdictions requires careful coordination of prosecution in multiple countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closely monitor office actions and legal developments in each jurisdiction to adapt claims while maintaining family claim scope overlap. Ensure consistent prosecution narratives and technical justifications across patent families to minimize invalidity risk and maximize retention of essentiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-issuance claim-chart mapping and portfolio hygiene
rubrics_metrics.description: After a patent issues, create a detailed claim chart that maps patented claims to the relevant sections of the technical standard to determine whether claims read on the standard and identify deficiencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For large or growing portfolios, build systems to track which patents correspond to each standard. Claim charts help determine deficiencies that may be addressed via continuations, divisionals, or reissue applications. Tracking as the portfolio develops is easier than retroactive sifting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declare patents/applications to SSOs appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Most SSOs require members to declare patents they own that could be essential to practicing a standard; the critical consideration is when to declare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing depends on the SSO—some prefer declarations when it’s 'credible' the application will be issued as an SEP, others prefer as early as possible. If unsure, contact the SSO to determine their preference. Declarations are typically made by patent holders who are SSO members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty optimization via understanding SSO licensing agreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Request from the relevant SSO a copy of a standard licensing agreement to learn how royalties are calculated and to optimize claiming strategies accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some SSO agreements base royalties on the number of assets licensed and reduce royalties once a threshold is reached (potentially per jurisdiction). Factor these limits into claim and portfolio strategies—e.g., target an ideal number of assets (example: 10 patents) and divide technology (server/client, encoder/decoder) across patents to hit that target.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent marking and virtual marking practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent marking is critical for monetization; marking products practicing a patent provides constructive notice and can affect damages recovery periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the U.S., marking permits recovery of damages up to six years prior to filing suit rather than from actual notice. Use physical marking or virtual marking (link to website with product/patent info). Claim charts assist in tracking which products should be marked and which competitor products practice which patents. Require licensees to mark relevant products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify licensing targets and 'proud patents' through monitoring and diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding who is likely to require a license starts with monitoring industries and standards development and performing internal diligence to identify high-value patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor SSO meetings, industry players, new entrants, and products that implement standards. Identify 'proud patents'—those with broad claims, strong essentiality reads, and low invalidity risk—as primary negotiation/leverage assets; proud SEPs can be charted before specific infringers are identified.

rubrics_metrics.name: SEP licensing negotiation practices and FRAND compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: SEP licensing negotiations should be conducted in good faith to comply with FRAND obligations, with the process typically centered on licensing terms and infringement/validity merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiations often begin with a letter explaining that SEPs are essential and inviting discussion; initial letters generally avoid naming specific patents to prevent triggering IPRs (e.g., IPR petitions or declaratory judgment actions). Discussions involve claim charts and financial talks over months or years. Maintain repeated, continuous communications to demonstrate good-faith negotiation. Whether an offer is FRAND-compliant depends on variables like comparable industry licenses and parties’ conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid naming specific patents in initial outreach to mitigate IPR risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial licensing letters generally do not name specific patents because doing so could enable the potential infringer to initiate inter partes review or declaratory judgment actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep initial communications descriptive (that SEPs are essential to standards practiced by the recipient) rather than listing patents. Be mindful that mutual SEP ownership can prompt reciprocal accusations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigation strategy: expect multi-jurisdictional, differing-timetable disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: If negotiations fail, SEP disputes often lead to litigation that is frequently global, with co-pending matters in multiple countries and differing procedural timelines and requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Faster proceedings (e.g., ITC in U.S., ex parte preliminary proceedings in Brazil/Colombia, fast German timelines) can influence outcomes elsewhere. Different jurisdictions may require separate invalidity proceedings. Monitor cross-border effects and prepare for coordination or tactical use of faster forums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement drafting should resolve global disputes and account for future standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Settlements typically aim to resolve all co-pending global disputes and should consider technology timetables and iterative nature of standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design settlements keyed to technology generations (e.g., settle 4G but leave 5G for later or set renegotiation dates for later technologies). Account for possible re-declarations of SEPs to future versions of standards and include mechanisms to address later-arising technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use experienced counsel with combined tech and legal expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: SEP strategy requires prescience, adaptability, and diligence uncommon even among sophisticated patent owners; shrewd legal counsel with a thorough command of both technology and law is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage counsel who understand the relevant technical standards, SSO practices, cross-jurisdictional prosecution/litigation nuances, FRAND jurisprudence, and licensing negotiations to maximize chances of successful SEP monetization and risk management.
